idiom_name: discriminated union of bound kinds over a generic Interval<T>
implementation_notes: TypeScript adds no runtime interval, but its type system is the reason to model bound kinds explicitly: type the interval as { lo: Bound<T>; hi: Bound<T> } with Bound<T> = { kind: 'closed' | 'open'; value: T } | { kind: 'unbounded' }, so contains/overlaps switch exhaustively over the bound kind and a missing side is a compile error rather than a runtime undefined. Comparisons still need a projection to a comparable primitive (ISO strings, epoch milliseconds) or an explicit comparator, because < on Dates or objects is not what domain code expects; and the type cannot carry a runtime dependency, so heavy time-range work adds Luxon's Interval typings on top. The runtime object is JavaScript's: keep it immutable (Readonly / Object.freeze) and agree on null vs absent for unbounded sides.
pitfalls: A structurally identical object literal can be passed where a closed interval is expected: if bound kinds are not part of the value (plain { lo, hi }), the compiler cannot stop a half-open range from being used as a closed one.
T with no comparability constraint is a lie: TypeScript happily accepts Date or a plain object, and the runtime comparison then uses string coercion or reference identity.
readonly is shallow: readonly lo: Bound<T> does not prevent mutating the bound object's value field, so intervals must be rebuilt rather than patched.
Exhaustiveness is only enforced where the switch is written; a default branch that returns false turns a future bound kind into a silent behaviour change instead of a compile error.
